paragraphs.heading: Distances that grow
paragraphs.text: The expansion of the universe means that, as time passes, the distances between parts of the observable universe that are not held together by gravity get larger. The expansion is built into space itself. It does not mean the universe is spreading into something, or that there is space outside it. The idea is hard to explain, and it has led to several misconceptions.

paragraphs.heading: What any observer sees
paragraphs.text: Wherever you stand in the universe, all but the closest galaxies seem to be moving away from you. On average, the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes, in proportion to its distance. The nearest galaxies are the exception because gravity binds them together. Nothing can travel faster than light, but that limit only applies locally, so it does not cap how fast very distant objects can recede.

paragraphs.heading: Found in the 1920s
paragraphs.text: Both theory and observation uncovered the expansion in the 1920s. Between 1912 and 1914 Vesto Slipher found that light from remote galaxies was redshifted, which was later read as a sign they are moving away from Earth. In 1922 Alexander Friedmann used Einstein's equations to show in theory that the universe is expanding. In 1927 Georges Lemaître used data from Slipher and Hubble to propose a straight-line link between a galaxy's distance and its speed of recession, and Edwin Hubble firmly established that link in 1929.

paragraphs.heading: Fast, slow, then fast again
paragraphs.text: The standard Lambda-CDM model says the expansion rate has changed over time, depending on what the universe contains. In the earliest stage, called inflation, the universe suddenly stretched at least 10²⁶ times over along each direction. After that the expansion slowed a great deal. Then, about 4 billion years ago, it began to speed up gradually, and it is still doing so. To explain this recent speed-up, physicists have proposed dark energy.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the size of it
paragraphs.text: Cosmologists track the expansion with a number called the scale factor, written a, which grows in step with the average spacing between objects such as galaxies. By convention a = 1 today, so it was smaller in the past and will be larger in the future. Running the clock backward in some models reaches a moment when the scale factor was zero, which current cosmology places 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years ago.

paragraphs.heading: A tug of war
paragraphs.text: One way to picture the expansion is that the universe's contents started out flying apart. The gravity of all the matter and radiation slowly holds the expansion back, but it is too thinly spread to stop it. On top of that, recent evidence suggests dark energy is now making the expansion speed up. If the expansion goes on forever, the scale factor will grow without limit, though in principle the universe could also stop and begin to shrink.
